items.title: Reject unsupported HTTP methods at every application route
items.objective: Determine whether unsupported methods reach a handler or bypass route-specific controls.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Capture the intended method and response for a representative route
Use OPTIONS only as a discovery hint
Repeat with one unsupported method while preserving identity and body
Compare status, response body, headers, and server-side state

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for reject unsupported http methods at every application route and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: Unsupported methods are rejected consistently, normally with 405 and an accurate Allow value.
items.vulnerable_behavior: An unsupported method reaches protected logic, returns sensitive data, or performs a state change.
items.validation: Verify server-side state and repeat with a baseline; a different status or generic page alone is insufficient.
false_positives: OPTIONS can be intentionally enabled for CORS
A framework can return 200 from a fallback route without invoking the target handler
items.impact: A verified method bypass can expose data or unauthorized functions.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata
items.remediation: Allowlist methods in routing and enforce authentication, authorization, and action semantics inside every handler.

items.title: Keep safe HTTP methods free of state-changing side effects
items.objective: Determine whether GET, HEAD, or OPTIONS can trigger a security-sensitive state change.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Identify sensitive mutations from normal workflows
Check whether any equivalent link or request uses a safe method
Send one safe-method request against a reversible test object
Compare authoritative state before and after

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for keep safe http methods free of state-changing side effects and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: Safe methods retrieve metadata or representations without changing application state.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A safe-method request changes account, object, payment, permission, or workflow state.
items.validation: Confirm the committed effect using a fresh read and exclude analytics or access-log writes.
false_positives: Servers naturally record access logs for GET
A GET can initialize non-security preferences without meaningful impact
items.impact: Unsafe GET behavior enables cross-site triggering, crawler activation, replay, and cache-related side effects.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata
items.remediation: Use POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE for mutations and require intent, authorization, and CSRF controls where browsers send ambient credentials.
items.safety: Use only reversible changes on designated test objects; never trigger payment, deletion, fulfillment, or notification side effects during this check.

items.title: Constrain HTTP method override mechanisms
items.objective: Determine whether override headers or body parameters permit unauthorized verbs or inconsistent controls.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Check normal traffic and framework documentation for override support
Send the intended request as a control
Add one observed override field for a different harmless method
Compare routing, authorization, response, and state

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for constrain http method override mechanisms and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: Overrides are disabled unless required, strictly allowlisted, and enter the same authorization path as the effective method.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A client-controlled override reaches a function denied through the normal method or bypasses intermediary controls.
items.validation: Prove the effective server action and preserve all inputs except the override signal.
false_positives: A proxy can strip the override before the application
The response can echo an override without changing the effective route
items.impact: Method override confusion can bypass gateway, routing, or function-level access controls.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata
items.remediation: Disable unnecessary overrides or normalize them once at a trusted edge before method allowlisting and authorization.

items.title: Require declared request media types to match parsed bodies
items.objective: Determine whether endpoints parse bodies under undeclared, ambiguous, or conflicting Content-Type values.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Capture a valid body and declared media type
Repeat with the media type removed
Repeat with one incompatible media type while preserving bytes
Compare validation, parser selection, and side effects

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for require declared request media types to match parsed bodies and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: Endpoints accept only documented media types and reject mismatches before business processing.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A mismatched declaration selects a weaker parser or bypasses validation/security middleware.
items.validation: Demonstrate a security-relevant interpretation difference; tolerant parsing by itself is not a vulnerability.
false_positives: Some endpoints intentionally support multiple documented media types
A generic 400 difference does not show a control bypass
items.impact: Parser selection inconsistencies can enable validation, CSRF, or data-binding bypasses.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata
items.remediation: Route bodies by an explicit media-type allowlist, reject ambiguity, and apply equivalent validation after parsing.

items.title: Send accurate response media types and safe character encodings
items.objective: Determine whether responses declare a media type and charset consistent with their actual bytes and browser context.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Capture representative HTML, JSON, XML, text, and download responses
Compare Content-Type with actual representation
Check explicit or format-defined character encoding
Observe browser handling only with harmless test content

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for send accurate response media types and safe character encodings and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: Every body has an accurate media type and a safe unambiguous encoding appropriate to the format.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A mismatch causes attacker-influenced bytes to be interpreted in an executable or less constrained context.
items.validation: Show actual browser or consumer interpretation and attacker control; a missing charset alone is not a finding.
false_positives: JSON has a defined Unicode encoding model without requiring a charset parameter
A browser can safely render plain text despite a generic server default
items.impact: Type or encoding confusion can turn inert data into active content or create parser differentials.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata
items.remediation: Set Content-Type from trusted route metadata, use UTF-8 consistently, and prevent user input from selecting response types.

items.title: Prevent browser MIME sniffing on active and user-controlled responses
items.objective: Determine whether browser sniffing can reinterpret a response as script, style, or HTML in a security-relevant load context.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Identify scripts, styles, downloads, API data, and user-controlled resources
Record Content-Type and X-Content-Type-Options
Load only a harmless controlled resource through its realistic destination context
Observe whether the browser blocks or reinterprets it

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for prevent browser mime sniffing on active and user-controlled responses and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: Responses declare accurate types and use nosniff where browser reinterpretation would create risk.
items.vulnerable_behavior: Attacker-controlled bytes execute or render actively because the browser ignores or overrides an unsafe declared type.
items.validation: Demonstrate the exact load context and execution/rendering effect; a missing header without a viable context is informational.
false_positives: Browsers do not sniff every destination or media type
A missing nosniff header can be irrelevant for fixed server-generated HTML
items.impact: Successful type confusion can enable script execution, content spoofing, or unsafe handling of uploads.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata
items.remediation: Set accurate media types, add X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, isolate user content, and force downloads when active rendering is unnecessary.

items.title: Normalize path segments before routing and authorization
items.objective: Determine whether dot segments, repeated separators, case, or trailing delimiters reach inconsistent handlers or controls.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Capture one authorized route as a baseline
Create one semantically equivalent path variant at a time
Compare edge and application status, handler identity, and authorization
Repeat only when the variant remains within the same approved route

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for normalize path segments before routing and authorization and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: All hops agree on one canonical path before routing, caching, and authorization.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A non-canonical path reaches protected content or a different control path than its canonical equivalent.
items.validation: Prove equivalent resource/handler identity and a security-relevant control difference.
false_positives: Case-sensitive paths can intentionally identify different resources
A redirect to the canonical path is generally secure behavior
items.impact: Canonicalization disagreement can bypass access controls, filters, or cache boundaries.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata
items.remediation: Canonicalize once at the trusted edge, reject ambiguous forms, and authorize the canonical route used by the application.

items.title: Decode percent-encoded and Unicode input exactly once
items.objective: Determine whether HTTP components disagree because a path or parameter is decoded multiple times or under different character rules.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Choose a harmless path or parameter with a known value
Send its canonical encoding as a control
Test one single- and double-encoded equivalent
Compare routing, validation, cache behavior, and final parsed value

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for decode percent-encoded and unicode input exactly once and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: Input is decoded once into a canonical form before validation and all downstream components use that form.
items.vulnerable_behavior: An alternate encoding bypasses a validation or routing decision and reaches a security-sensitive interpretation.
items.validation: Trace the final value or resource and repeat controls; response differences alone do not establish double decoding.
false_positives: Different encoded forms can be rejected by design
A WAF can block encoding while the application never receives it
items.impact: Decode disagreement can enable traversal, filter bypass, duplicate resources, and parser confusion.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata
items.remediation: Define accepted encodings, decode once before validation, reject malformed sequences, and align edge and application parsers.

items.title: Resolve duplicate HTTP parameters consistently
items.objective: Determine how every hop handles repeated names and whether inconsistent first/last/list semantics bypass controls.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Capture a single-valued harmless parameter
Repeat its name with the same value as a control
Send two distinct safe values in both orders
Compare gateway validation, application value, logs, and response

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for resolve duplicate http parameters consistently and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: Duplicate names are rejected or interpreted under one documented rule shared by all components.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A security control inspects one value while downstream logic acts on another.
items.validation: Demonstrate the conflicting values at two trust boundaries or a resulting control bypass.
false_positives: Frameworks can intentionally expose repeated values as an array
A response difference can reflect ordinary multi-select behavior
items.impact: Parameter pollution can bypass validation, authorization, signatures, cache keys, or business rules.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Testing for HTTP Parameter Pollution

items.remediation: Use typed input contracts, reject unexpected duplicates, and normalize parameter semantics before security decisions.

items.title: Handle absolute-form and authority-form request targets safely
items.objective: Determine whether proxy-style absolute targets or authority forms alter routing, host validation, or generated links.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Capture an origin-form HTTP/1.1 request
Repeat with an absolute-form target containing the same authority
Where supported, compare authority and Host conflict handling
Observe routing and generated URLs without using external destinations

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for handle absolute-form and authority-form request targets safely and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: Unsupported target forms are rejected; supported proxy forms use one validated authority consistently.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A conflicting target authority changes routing, cache identity, password-reset links, or a security decision.
items.validation: Prove the server-selected authority through a harmless same-scope effect; parser acceptance alone is insufficient.
false_positives: Forward proxies legitimately require absolute-form targets
Servers can normalize absolute form to the same origin without risk
items.impact: Authority ambiguity can enable host-routing, cache, or link-generation attacks.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata
items.remediation: Reject unexpected request-target forms and derive authority from one trusted, allowlisted source after proxy normalization.

items.title: Keep HTTP/1 Host and HTTP/2 authority validation equivalent
items.objective: Determine whether Host and :authority reach different virtual hosts or security policies across protocol versions.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Capture equivalent HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 requests
Compare canonical authority handling
Where tooling permits safely, send conflicting Host and :authority values using approved names
Compare rejection, routing, redirects, and cache behavior

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for keep http/1 host and http/2 authority validation equivalent and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: Every protocol version validates one canonical approved authority and rejects conflicts.
items.vulnerable_behavior: Protocol-specific authority parsing reaches a different application or bypasses host-dependent controls.
items.validation: Demonstrate a same-scope routing/control difference and exclude client translation artifacts.
false_positives: Clients and proxies can rewrite one authority field before transmission
HTTP/2 libraries may prohibit constructing an invalid conflict
items.impact: Authority discrepancies can bypass routing, tenant boundaries, or cache partitioning.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata
items.remediation: Normalize authority at the trusted edge, reject conflicts, and apply the same host allowlist across HTTP versions.

items.title: Trust forwarding headers only from authenticated intermediaries
items.objective: Determine whether clients can influence scheme, host, address, or path values that the application expects a proxy to set.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Identify forwarding headers used in normal edge traffic
Send a baseline through the intended public path
Add one client-supplied conflicting forwarded value
Observe redirects, links, access decisions, rate identity, and logs

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for trust forwarding headers only from authenticated intermediaries and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: The edge strips client values and sets trusted forwarding metadata; the application trusts only authenticated proxy hops.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A client value controls a security-relevant scheme, host, IP, or path decision.
items.validation: Show a concrete downstream effect and verify the value was not merely reflected in diagnostics.
false_positives: Applications can log untrusted forwarded values without acting on them
A CDN can overwrite the test header before it reaches the application
items.impact: Forwarded-header trust can enable host injection, HTTPS confusion, IP control bypass, or poisoned links.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata
items.remediation: Strip inbound forwarding headers at the edge, set canonical values, authenticate internal hops, and parse only a configured proxy chain.

items.title: Restrict user-controlled redirects to approved destinations
items.objective: Determine whether redirect parameters, paths, or headers can send users to an attacker-controlled origin.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Capture a normal same-origin redirect
Identify the destination input and accepted representation
Substitute a controlled HTTPS destination using one syntax at a time
Confirm the browser's final effective origin without collecting credentials

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for restrict user-controlled redirects to approved destinations and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: Redirect destinations are fixed, relative, or matched exactly against an approved allowlist; external transitions are clearly mediated.
items.vulnerable_behavior: Attacker-controlled input places an unapproved origin in an automatic redirect Location or equivalent navigation.
items.validation: Use a controlled domain and prove final browser navigation; reflected text or a rejected error page is insufficient.
false_positives: A warning/interstitial can intentionally permit user-approved external links
A destination can be a separately approved partner allowlist entry
items.impact: Open redirects support phishing, OAuth flow abuse, and trust-boundary confusion.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata
items.remediation: Use relative destinations or stable identifiers mapped server-side; otherwise exact-allowlist destinations and clearly warn for external navigation.
items.safety: Use only a controlled non-lookalike HTTPS destination and never collect credentials, tokens, or real-user traffic.

items.title: Redirect browser-facing HTTP requests to canonical HTTPS safely
items.objective: Determine whether plaintext entry paths expose sensitive content or redirect inconsistently before HTTPS enforcement.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Request representative browser-facing routes over HTTP without credentials
Record status, body, cookies, and Location
Verify the redirect targets the canonical HTTPS host and preserves only safe path data
Test APIs separately because transparent redirects may be inappropriate

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for redirect browser-facing http requests to canonical https safely and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: Browser routes redirect before sensitive processing and emit no secrets/cookies over plaintext; non-browser services fail or upgrade according to contract.
items.vulnerable_behavior: Plain HTTP serves sensitive content, accepts credentials, or redirects to an unsafe host with a realistic interception path.
items.validation: Demonstrate exposed data or action without sending real secrets; a non-redirecting API is not automatically vulnerable.
false_positives: APIs may intentionally reject HTTP rather than redirect
Local health endpoints can be unreachable from attacker networks
items.impact: Plaintext handling can expose credentials, tokens, content, or redirect integrity to network attackers.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Testing for Weak Transport Layer Security

items.remediation: Disable plaintext at the edge where possible, redirect only browser endpoints canonically, mark cookies Secure, and use HSTS after HTTPS readiness.

items.title: Allowlist CORS origins without substring or reflection mistakes
items.objective: Determine whether Access-Control-Allow-Origin is fixed or derived from an exact approved origin policy.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Capture a CORS response for an intended application origin
Repeat with a controlled untrusted origin
Test one suffix, prefix, and scheme/port variation relevant to the allowlist
Check ACAO and whether the browser exposes the response

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for allowlist cors origins without substring or reflection mistakes and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: Only exact approved scheme-host-port origins receive ACAO and unapproved origins receive no readable grant.
items.vulnerable_behavior: An untrusted controlled origin is granted read access to a security-sensitive response.
items.validation: Use a real browser fetch and prove sensitive readable data; header reflection alone may lack credentials or sensitive content.
false_positives: Wildcard ACAO is valid for intentionally public non-credentialed resources
A server can emit ACAO while the browser blocks due to another CORS rule
items.impact: CORS allowlist errors can disclose authenticated or network-restricted data cross-origin.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Testing Cross Origin Resource Sharing

items.remediation: Compare parsed origins by exact scheme, host, and port against a fixed allowlist; never use substring, suffix-only, or blind reflection checks.

items.title: Reject credentialed CORS access from untrusted origins
items.objective: Determine whether browsers can read user-specific responses cross-origin with ambient cookies or HTTP authentication.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Identify a harmless response that differs by test identity
Fetch it from the intended origin as a control
Repeat from a controlled untrusted origin with browser credentials mode enabled
Record ACAO, ACAC, SameSite behavior, and readable response data

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for reject credentialed cors access from untrusted origins and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: Credentialed reads are granted only to exact trusted origins and sensitive responses remain unreadable elsewhere.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A controlled untrusted origin can read a victim-context response containing non-public data.
items.validation: Prove JavaScript can read identity-specific content in a browser; cookies being sent or a 200 response alone is insufficient.
false_positives: SameSite cookies may prevent ambient credentials on the tested cross-site request
A response can be public and identical for every user
items.impact: Credentialed CORS abuse can expose account or tenant data to an attacker-controlled site.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Testing Cross Origin Resource Sharing

steps: Verify actual SameSite cookie behavior for the exact fetch context before concluding credentials are available.
variants.notes: ACAC does not override browser cookie policy.

steps: Determine whether client code would attach the bearer token for the untrusted origin; Authorization headers are not ambient browser credentials.
variants.notes: A header-only token usually requires a separate token exposure or trusted client behavior.

items.remediation: Use an exact origin allowlist, minimize credentialed CORS, set purpose-appropriate SameSite cookies, and authorize every resource server-side.

items.title: Treat opaque and null origins according to explicit threat models
items.objective: Determine whether Origin: null is trusted where sandboxed documents, local files, redirects, or opaque origins can reach sensitive resources.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Confirm whether the application intentionally supports opaque origins
Send a control request with an intended origin
Repeat with Origin: null
If granted, reproduce from a controlled sandboxed document and test only harmless data

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for treat opaque and null origins according to explicit threat models and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: Null is rejected unless a documented use case requires it and compensating controls prevent access to sensitive data.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A controlled opaque-origin page can read a sensitive response because null is broadly trusted.
items.validation: Demonstrate a browser-reachable null-origin context and readable sensitive data; a header alone is insufficient.
false_positives: Native or file-based clients can legitimately require null-origin support
The resource can be intentionally public and non-credentialed
items.impact: Trusting null broadly can expose data to sandboxed attacker-controlled documents or local-origin contexts.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Testing Cross Origin Resource Sharing

items.remediation: Avoid allowlisting null for sensitive resources; use explicit authenticated clients, scoped capabilities, and non-browser channels for exceptional cases.

items.title: Apply equivalent controls to simple and preflighted cross-origin requests
items.objective: Determine whether a sensitive operation becomes reachable by changing method or media type so the browser skips CORS preflight.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Capture the normal state-changing request and its preflight requirements
Construct an equivalent safe test using a CORS-safelisted method/media type where the endpoint accepts it
Send from a controlled origin with a reversible test object
Verify server-side state and browser readability separately

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for apply equivalent controls to simple and preflighted cross-origin requests and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: Sensitive operations require an attacker-unavailable signal or reject alternate simple request shapes independent of preflight.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A controlled origin triggers a sensitive action by choosing a request shape that avoids preflight and other intent checks.
items.validation: Confirm the committed effect in a browser and exclude operations protected by CSRF tokens, SameSite, or reauthentication.
false_positives: CORS blocks response reading but does not itself prevent request sending
A simple request can be accepted syntactically yet rejected before state change
items.impact: Preflight assumptions can enable cross-site state changes or alternate-parser control bypass.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Testing Cross Origin Resource Sharing

items.remediation: Do not use preflight as the sole CSRF defense; restrict media types/methods and require origin-bound anti-forgery signals for ambient credentials.
items.safety: Use a reversible action on a designated account and restore state immediately; never test payments, deletion, or real-user communication.

items.title: Avoid exposing sensitive response headers cross-origin
items.objective: Determine whether Access-Control-Expose-Headers reveals secrets or sensitive metadata to origins that can read a response.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Inventory non-safelisted response headers used by browser clients
Record Access-Control-Expose-Headers for trusted and untrusted origins
Fetch a harmless identity-specific response from a controlled origin
Check which header values JavaScript can read

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for avoid exposing sensitive response headers cross-origin and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: Only necessary non-sensitive headers are exposed and only to approved origins.
items.vulnerable_behavior: An untrusted origin can read a token, internal identifier, signed URL, or other security-sensitive header.
items.validation: Demonstrate JavaScript access and explain the header's security use; header names alone do not prove impact.
false_positives: Pagination and request-ID headers are commonly safe to expose
An exposed header can contain only public metadata
items.impact: Sensitive exposed headers can leak credentials, capabilities, internal identifiers, or tenant metadata.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Testing Cross Origin Resource Sharing

items.remediation: Minimize exposed headers, never place reusable secrets in response headers readable by clients, and combine with exact origin policy.

items.title: Prevent sensitive browser responses from persistent caching
items.objective: Determine whether browsers retain authenticated or sensitive representations after logout or on shared devices.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Select a sensitive but non-destructive test-account response
Record Cache-Control, Pragma where legacy support matters, and browser storage behavior
Navigate away, use back/forward, then log out
Check whether content is restored without a fresh authorized request

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for prevent sensitive browser responses from persistent caching and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: Sensitive responses use no-store where required and are not recoverable after session invalidation on the tested browser.
items.vulnerable_behavior: Sensitive account data remains available from browser cache after logout or to a subsequent local user.
items.validation: Prove retrieval without a network authorization check and assess the shared-device threat model.
false_positives: Memory rendering during the same active session can be expected
Back navigation can trigger a fresh authorized request rather than cache reuse
items.impact: Persistent browser caching can expose account data on shared or compromised local devices.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Testing for Browser Cache Weaknesses

items.remediation: Use Cache-Control: no-store for sensitive responses, clear client state on logout, and avoid embedding secrets in cacheable pages.

items.title: Partition shared caches by identity and authorization context
items.objective: Determine whether a CDN, reverse proxy, or server cache can serve one user's representation to another.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Choose a harmless response that differs between two designated accounts
Prime it as account A using a unique test object
Request the same cache key as account B and unauthenticated
Repeat controls while recording Age, cache-status, Vary, and body identity

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for partition shared caches by identity and authorization context and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: Private responses are not shared, or cache partitions include every identity/authorization dimension needed to prevent cross-user reuse.
items.vulnerable_behavior: Account B receives account A's non-public representation from a shared cache.
items.validation: Use unique canary data and repeated A/B controls to distinguish caching from an underlying authorization flaw.
false_positives: The origin itself can return the wrong object without a cache being involved
A cache header can be synthesized even on a miss
items.impact: Cross-user cache leakage can disclose account or tenant data at scale.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata
items.remediation: Mark private data non-shared, remove it from edge caching, or use a safe server-controlled partition key while still enforcing origin authorization.
items.safety: Use only designated accounts and synthetic canary data; stop immediately if any unrelated user's content appears.

items.title: Include every response-shaping input in shared cache keys
items.objective: Determine whether unkeyed query fields, headers, cookies, or path transformations let one request poison another response.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Identify a cacheable harmless route and establish miss/hit behavior
Change one response-shaping input using a unique inert marker
Request the baseline cache key without that input
Check whether the marker persists for a clean control request

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for include every response-shaping input in shared cache keys and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: Inputs that affect the response are keyed, stripped, normalized safely, or make the response uncacheable.
items.vulnerable_behavior: An unkeyed attacker-controlled input persists in a cached response served to clean requests.
items.validation: Require a reproducible miss-prime-hit sequence with a unique harmless marker and exclude origin persistence.
false_positives: The marker can be reflected by the origin on every request rather than cached
Different edge nodes can produce inconsistent cache observations
items.impact: Cache poisoning can distribute redirects, script references, content spoofing, or security-policy changes to many users.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata
items.remediation: Define cache keys from canonical request semantics, strip untrusted response-shaping inputs, and never cache responses influenced by unkeyed data.
items.safety: Use an isolated route or cache-buster approved by the owner, an inert marker, one prime/control sequence, and purge immediately if persistence occurs.

items.title: Send correct Vary metadata for negotiated cacheable responses
items.objective: Determine whether caches distinguish representations shaped by safe request headers such as Origin, Accept-Encoding, or language.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Identify a route whose response changes by a request header
Request two variants with unique harmless context
Record Vary and cache-status metadata
Alternate requests and verify each receives its intended representation

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for send correct vary metadata for negotiated cacheable responses and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: Vary accurately names every supported request field that selects a cacheable representation, or the response is not shared.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A cache reuses security-relevant CORS, encoding, locale, or content variants across requests that require separation.
items.validation: Prove cross-variant reuse and meaningful impact; a missing Vary value without cache reuse is not a finding.
false_positives: The CDN can key a field through configuration without emitting Vary
A response difference can be generated after the shared cache
items.impact: Incorrect variation can leak data, corrupt CORS policy, or cause content and encoding confusion.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata
items.remediation: Align cache configuration and Vary metadata with actual negotiation, and disable shared caching when safe partitioning cannot be guaranteed.

items.title: Reauthorize conditional and range requests for protected resources
items.objective: Determine whether If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since, or Range can retrieve metadata or bytes without the authorization required for a full response.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Capture an authorized protected-resource response and validators
Repeat as another designated identity with conditional headers
Request one small byte range where the resource supports ranges
Compare authorization before interpreting 206 or 304 semantics

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for reauthorize conditional and range requests for protected resources and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: Authorization runs before conditional/range handling and unauthorized callers receive no validator or content oracle.
items.vulnerable_behavior: An unauthorized caller receives protected bytes or a reliable existence/change oracle through 206, 304, ETag, or Last-Modified behavior.
items.validation: Confirm ownership and compare with a nonexistent control; validators can be opaque and non-sensitive.
false_positives: A 304 to an already authorized browser can be normal
Public static files legitimately support ranges and validators
items.impact: Bypasses can disclose protected file content or reveal existence and modification state.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata
items.remediation: Authorize the resource first, then evaluate conditions/ranges, and avoid stable cross-user validators for private representations.
items.safety: Request only a tiny range from a synthetic test resource and avoid repeated multipart ranges or large-file amplification.

items.title: Disable compression where reflected secrets create a practical oracle
items.objective: Determine whether cross-request response-size observations can reveal secrets compressed alongside attacker-controlled input.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Identify responses containing both a test secret and reflected controllable text
Confirm response compression and stable size behavior
Use a very small set of benign guesses against a synthetic secret
Evaluate whether an attacker can repeat observations in the real browser/network context

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for disable compression where reflected secrets create a practical oracle and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: Secrets are not compressed in a practical attacker-observable reflection context, or masking and request isolation remove the oracle.
items.vulnerable_behavior: Repeated attacker-controlled requests yield a stable size signal correlated with a secret prefix under realistic conditions.
items.validation: Require a synthetic secret, repeatable statistics, and a feasible attacker request/observation model; compression alone is not vulnerable.
false_positives: Dynamic padding and unrelated response variance can destroy the oracle
An attacker may be unable to trigger authenticated requests or observe compressed lengths
items.impact: A practical compression oracle can disclose CSRF tokens or other response secrets over many observations.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata
items.remediation: Disable compression for affected secret-bearing responses, separate secrets from reflected input, rotate per-request secrets, and add masking or padding as defense in depth.
items.safety: Use only a synthetic secret and a strict request ceiling in an approved window; stop if latency or error rate changes.

items.title: Keep HTTP framing and protocol translation unambiguous
items.objective: Determine whether normal edge-to-origin protocol translation rejects conflicting message length and malformed framing before application processing.
prerequisites: A representative in-scope endpoint
A designated test account or public control route
steps: Confirm the public and upstream HTTP versions with the owner
Send well-formed Content-Length and chunked controls separately
In an isolated or approved window, send one conflict expected to be rejected
Verify no follow-up response, queue, or connection anomaly occurs

examples.note: Use a unique inert marker for keep http framing and protocol translation unambiguous and preserve a clean baseline.

items.manipulate: One HTTP semantic at a time while preserving route, identity, and all unrelated request values
items.secure_behavior: The edge rejects ambiguous framing and translates HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 to unambiguous upstream messages.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A controlled paired probe shows components disagree on message boundaries or a conflicting request reaches application logic.
items.validation: One timeout is not proof; require repeatable paired controls and isolated confirmation before classifying desynchronization.
false_positives: WAF rejection, retries, and backend latency can cause anomalous timing
Client libraries can normalize conflicting headers before sending
items.impact: Framing disagreement can enable request smuggling, response queue poisoning, and security-control bypass.
evidence: Paired responses with timing and cache metadata

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Testing for HTTP Splitting and Smuggling

items.remediation: Reject conflicting framing at the first hop, align patched parsers, avoid unsafe downgrade behavior, and use one canonical message boundary.
items.safety: REVIEW ONLY. Prefer an isolated environment, send one paired probe at a time, avoid shared-user routes, and stop on any queue, latency, or response anomaly.
